questions.stem: A mother with a mitochondrial DNA mutation causing a myopathy has children who all inherit the mutation, while an affected father's children never inherit the mutation from him. This inheritance pattern is explained by which of the following?
options: Mitochondrial DNA follows X-linked recessive inheritance
Mitochondrial mutations only occur in homoplasmic states
Sperm mitochondria are eliminated from the embryo after fertilization
explanations: Incorrect: mitochondrial DNA is extranuclear and inherited maternally, unrelated to the X chromosome or X-linked inheritance patterns.

Incorrect: mitochondrial mutations can occur in either homoplasmic (all mitochondria mutated) or heteroplasmic (mixed) states; heteroplasmy actually produces the more variable clinical expression, not an exclusion of mutation occurrence.

Incorrect: genomic imprinting refers to parent-of-origin-specific silencing of certain nuclear genes (e.g., in Prader-Willi/Angelman syndromes), a distinct mechanism from maternal-only mitochondrial inheritance.

Correct: mitochondrial DNA is inherited exclusively from the mother because sperm mitochondria are eliminated from the embryo after fertilization, so an affected father cannot transmit mitochondrial disease to his offspring while a homoplasmic affected mother transmits it to all her children.
questions.overview: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited exclusively from the mother, since sperm mitochondria are eliminated after fertilization; a homoplasmic affected mother transmits the mutation to all children, while an affected father transmits it to none. Clinical severity varies with heteroplasmy (the proportion of mutant vs normal mitochondrial DNA) and tissue distribution, with muscle and CNS most often affected due to high aerobic metabolic demand (e.g., ragged red fibers in mitochondrial myopathies).

questions.stem: The ABO blood group system, in which AB individuals express both A and B antigens on red blood cells, is a classic example of which genetic phenomenon?
explanations: Incorrect: pleiotropy refers to one gene producing multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects, not two alleles both being expressed at one locus.
Correct: codominance occurs when both alleles are fully and independently expressed in the phenotype, exactly as seen with A and B antigens both expressed in AB individuals.
Incorrect: genetic anticipation refers to worsening severity across generations in trinucleotide repeat disorders, unrelated to blood group inheritance.
Incorrect: incomplete penetrance refers to some individuals with a disease-causing genotype not expressing the phenotype at all, unrelated to simultaneous expression of two alleles.
questions.overview: Codominance describes a genotype in which two different alleles are both fully expressed in the phenotype, as exemplified by the ABO blood group system, where AB heterozygotes express both A and B antigens on red blood cells rather than a blended or single dominant phenotype.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with a history of poor feeding and hypotonia at birth is now noted by parents to have an insatiable appetite and is gaining weight rapidly. Genetic testing shows loss of function of a gene on chromosome 15 that is normally expressed only from the paternal allele. Which of the following mechanisms is most consistent with this condition?
options: X-linked recessive inheritance of a mutated gene
Deletion of the maternal copy of chromosome 15q11-q13
Meiosis II nondisjunction resulting in trisomy 15
Trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene
Deletion of the paternal copy of chromosome 15q11-q13
explanations: Incorrect: Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by an imprinting/chromosome 15 abnormality, not X-linked inheritance.
Incorrect: deletion of the maternal copy affecting UBE3A causes Angelman syndrome, not Prader-Willi syndrome.
Incorrect: Prader-Willi syndrome is due to an imprinting/deletion defect, not aneuploidy such as trisomy 15.
Incorrect: FMR1 trinucleotide repeat expansion causes Fragile X syndrome, an unrelated X-linked disorder.

Correct: Prader-Willi syndrome results most commonly (~75%) from deletion of the paternally inherited copy of the PWS gene region on 15q11-q13, since it is normally only expressed from the paternal allele; the remaining ~25% arise from maternal uniparental disomy.
questions.overview: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of the paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13, most commonly via paternal deletion (~75%) or maternal uniparental disomy (~25%). It causes neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, followed by childhood hyperphagia/obesity, mild intellectual disability, and hypogonadism.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated for delayed puberty. He is tall with long limbs, has sparse facial hair, and gynecomastia. Testicular exam reveals small, firm testes. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Which of the following hormonal patterns is most likely?
options: Decreased FSH and LH, decreased testosterone
Increased FSH and LH, decreased testosterone
Increased FSH and LH, increased testosterone
Decreased FSH and LH, increased testosterone
Normal FSH and LH, decreased testosterone
explanations: Incorrect: describes secondary (central) hypogonadism, not the primary testicular failure of Klinefelter syndrome.
Correct: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary hypogonadism with seminiferous tubule/Leydig cell dysfunction: decreased testosterone (↑LH) and decreased inhibin B (↑FSH).
Incorrect: testosterone is low, not elevated, in Klinefelter syndrome due to Leydig cell/testicular dysfunction.
Incorrect: this pattern does not match Klinefelter syndrome physiology; both values move in the opposite direction from what is described.
Incorrect: loss of negative feedback from the testes causes elevated, not normal, gonadotropins.
questions.overview: Klinefelter syndrome (usually 47,XXY) results from meiotic nondisjunction and causes primary hypogonadism: small firm testes, low testosterone, elevated LH and FSH (from loss of inhibin B feedback), gynecomastia, infertility, and a tall eunuchoid body habitus from an extra SHOX gene copy.

questions.stem: An X-linked recessive disease affects 1 in 100 males in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Assuming equal allele frequencies in males and females, what is the approximate frequency of affected (homozygous) females?
explanations: Incorrect: 1 in 100 is the frequency of affected males (q), not the squared value (q²) needed for affected homozygous females.

Correct: among males, allele frequency q = frequency of affected males = 1/100 = 0.01; since males and females share the same allele frequencies, affected female frequency = q² = (0.01)² = 0.0001 = 1 in 10,000.
Incorrect: 1 in 50 is higher than the male disease frequency and does not reflect the correct squaring needed for female homozygotes.
Incorrect: 1 in 200 does not correspond to the correct q² calculation for this allele frequency.
questions.overview: For X-linked diseases, males (XY) have only one allele copy, so disease frequency in males directly equals the allele frequency q. Because affected females require two copies (homozygous, q²), X-linked recessive diseases are always far less common in females than males — a key reason conditions like hemophilia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy predominantly affect males.

questions.stem: A newborn has microphthalmia, cleft lip and palate, postaxial polydactyly, and a congenital heart defect. Brain imaging shows failure of separation of the cerebral hemispheres. Which trisomy is most likely responsible for this presentation?
explanations: Incorrect: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) presents with a flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, and endocardial cushion defects, not holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, or polydactyly.

Correct: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) classically presents with microphthalmia/anophthalmia, cleft lip/palate, postaxial polydactyly, holoprosencephaly (failure of cerebral hemisphere separation), and congenital heart defects; median survival is only about 7 days.
Incorrect: Edward syndrome (trisomy 18) presents with clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rockerbottom feet, micrognathia, and a prominent occiput, rather than holoprosencephaly and polydactyly.
Incorrect: trisomy 8 is not a classically described high-yield trisomy syndrome in these notes and does not match this constellation of findings.
questions.overview: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is a rare, severe trisomy with holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia/anophthalmia, cleft lip/palate, and postaxial polydactyly, along with congenital heart defects (VSD, PDA, ASD). Like trisomy 18, it is associated with advanced maternal age and carries a poor prognosis, with most infants dying within the first year of life.

questions.stem: Compared to Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Becker muscular dystrophy is characterized by which type of DMD gene mutation, resulting in a milder clinical course?
options: Complete deletion of the entire DMD gene
Non-frameshift (in-frame) deletion allowing partial dystrophin function
Frameshift deletion causing a premature stop codon
explanations: Incorrect: complete deletion of the entire DMD gene would be expected to abolish all dystrophin production, more consistent with a severe Duchenne-like phenotype, not the milder Becker form.

Correct: Becker muscular dystrophy results from non-frameshift (in-frame) mutations in the DMD gene, preserving the reading frame and allowing production of a partially functional, though abnormal, dystrophin protein, leading to milder disease with later onset than Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Incorrect: trinucleotide repeat expansion is not the mechanism of either Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy; these are caused by deletions in the DMD gene affecting the reading frame.
Incorrect: a frameshift mutation causing a premature stop codon and absent/truncated dystrophin describes Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the more severe form, not Becker.
questions.overview: Both Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy are X-linked recessive disorders caused by mutations in the DMD gene (encoding dystrophin), but Duchenne results from frameshift mutations causing absent/truncated protein and severe early-onset disease, while Becker results from non-frameshift (in-frame) mutations preserving partial dystrophin function and producing a later-onset, milder disease course.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought in because his parents noticed he uses his hands to push himself up from a seated position on the floor. Examination shows enlarged calves and proximal muscle weakness greater in the lower extremities. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. Genetic testing reveals a deletion in the DMD gene that disrupts the reading frame. Which of the following best describes the expected protein finding?
options: Normal dystrophin protein with abnormal alpha-dystroglycan
Absent or severely truncated dystrophin protein
Full-length but structurally abnormal dystrophin protein with partial function
Normal dystrophin with a separate defect in laminin
explanations: Incorrect: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a loss-of-function disorder; dystrophin expression is absent or markedly reduced, not increased.
Incorrect: dystroglycan itself is not the primary defect in dystrophinopathies; the primary defect is in dystrophin, which normally links intracellular actin to dystroglycan.

Correct: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by frameshift mutations in the DMD gene, producing a premature stop codon and absent/truncated, essentially nonfunctional dystrophin, explaining the severe phenotype (Gower's sign, pseudohypertrophy, elevated CK).

Incorrect: a full-length but abnormal, partially functional protein describes Becker muscular dystrophy, which results from non-frameshift (in-frame) mutations, not the frameshift mutation described here.

Incorrect: laminin is part of the extracellular matrix linked to dystrophin via dystroglycan, but the primary genetic defect described (frameshift DMD mutation) affects dystrophin, not laminin directly.
questions.overview: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by frameshift mutations in the massive DMD gene, leading to absent dystrophin and severe, early-onset proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, elevated CK, and Gower's sign. Becker muscular dystrophy results from non-frameshift mutations that preserve partial dystrophin function and cause milder disease.

questions.stem: A patient with neurofibromatosis type 1 has only mild skin findings, while his son with the same gene mutation has both skin findings and brain tumors. All family members carrying the mutation show at least some manifestation of disease. This pattern illustrates which of the following?
explanations: Incorrect: incomplete penetrance would mean some carriers show no disease features at all, which is not the case here since all family members show at least some manifestation.

Correct: NF1 is a classic example of a disorder with complete penetrance (100% of gene carriers show some disease manifestation) but variable expressivity (the severity/type of manifestations differs among individuals).
Incorrect: locus heterogeneity refers to different genes causing the same phenotype, which is not what is being illustrated (this is a single gene with variable severity).
Incorrect: genetic anticipation describes worsening severity/earlier onset across generations due to expanding trinucleotide repeats, which is not described in this scenario.
questions.overview: Penetrance describes the proportion of individuals with a disease genotype who show any phenotype, while expressivity describes the degree/severity of phenotype among those affected. Neurofibromatosis type 1 has 100% penetrance but highly variable expressivity, whereas BRCA1/2 mutations show incomplete penetrance for cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in both eyes. Family history reveals that his father was treated for a similar eye tumor as a child. Genetic testing shows a germline mutation in one copy of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene in all of the boy's cells. Which of the following best explains why this child developed bilateral tumors at a young age?
options: Mitochondrial inheritance from the father caused the phenotype
Trinucleotide repeat expansion in the RB1 gene explains the earlier age of onset
Two independent somatic mutations must occur in the same retinal cell for tumor formation
A single additional somatic mutation in the remaining normal RB1 allele is sufficient to cause tumor formation in retinal cells
The germline mutation alone is sufficient to cause malignant transformation without any additional mutation
explanations: Incorrect: retinoblastoma is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern at the pedigree level (though recessive at the cellular level) via a germline nuclear RB1 mutation, not mitochondrial inheritance.
Incorrect: retinoblastoma is not a trinucleotide repeat disorder; the two-hit tumor suppressor mechanism explains the disease, not repeat expansion.

Incorrect: requiring two independent somatic hits in the same cell describes the sporadic (non-hereditary) form of retinoblastoma, which typically causes a single, later-onset tumor, not this hereditary presentation.

Correct: in hereditary retinoblastoma, one 'hit' (mutation) is already present in the germline in every cell, so only one additional somatic 'hit' in the other allele is needed for loss of heterozygosity and tumor formation; this explains earlier onset and bilateral, multifocal tumors.

Incorrect: retinoblastoma is a recessive process at the cellular level; a single functional RB1 allele is still sufficient to prevent tumor formation, so the germline mutation alone is not sufficient without loss of the second allele.
questions.overview: Retinoblastoma illustrates the 'two-hit' model of tumor suppressor gene inactivation: the hereditary form has one germline RB1 mutation present in every cell, requiring only one somatic 'hit' for cancer, producing earlier-onset, often bilateral/multifocal tumors, whereas the sporadic form requires two somatic hits in the same cell and typically presents as a single, later tumor.

questions.stem: A newborn has a high-pitched, cat-like cry, microcephaly, widely set eyes, and a ventricular septal defect. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely responsible?
options: Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7
Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 22
Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
explanations: Incorrect: deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7, including the elastin gene, causes Williams syndrome, characterized by an elfin facies and supravalvular aortic stenosis, not a cat-like cry.
Incorrect: deletion of the long arm of chromosome 22 (22q11) causes DiGeorge syndrome, with thymic aplasia, hypocalcemia, and conotruncal heart defects, not a cat-like cry.

Correct: cri-du-chat syndrome ('5p- syndrome') results from deletion of part of the short arm of chromosome 5 and presents with a characteristic high-pitched, cat-like ('mewing') cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism, and congenital heart defects such as VSD.
Incorrect: trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) presents with holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, and microphthalmia, not the classic cat-like cry described here.
questions.overview: Cri-du-chat syndrome ('5p- syndrome') results from a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 and presents with a characteristic high-pitched, cat-like cry in infancy, severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, hypertelorism, and congenital heart defects (VSD, PDA, tetralogy of Fallot).

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought in for primary amenorrhea. She is short for her age and has a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Echocardiogram reveals a bicuspid aortic valve. Pelvic ultrasound shows bilateral streaks of fibrous tissue in place of ovaries. Laboratory studies would most likely show which of the following?
options: Increased LH and FSH with decreased estrogen
Decreased LH and FSH with decreased estrogen
Decreased LH and FSH with increased estrogen
Normal LH and FSH with decreased estrogen
Increased LH and FSH with increased estrogen
explanations: Correct: Turner syndrome (streak ovaries/gonadal dysgenesis) causes primary hypogonadism, so decreased estrogen and inhibin B removes negative feedback, causing increased LH/FSH.
Incorrect: decreased gonadotropins would suggest a central (hypothalamic/pituitary) cause of hypogonadism, not the primary ovarian failure seen in Turner syndrome.
Incorrect: both estrogen and gonadotropins would be low only in central hypogonadism, which is not the mechanism in Turner syndrome.
Incorrect: loss of ovarian follicles removes negative feedback, so gonadotropins are elevated, not normal.
Incorrect: estrogen is decreased, not increased, due to ovarian failure (streak ovaries) in Turner syndrome.
questions.overview: Turner syndrome (45,X in ~45% of cases) causes short stature (loss of the SHOX gene), a webbed neck, a shield chest with widely spaced nipples, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, and horseshoe kidney. Gonadal dysgenesis ('streak ovaries') produces primary hypogonadism with decreased estrogen/inhibin B and increased LH/FSH, causing primary amenorrhea.

questions.stem: The risk of trisomy 21 due to meiotic nondisjunction increases significantly with advanced maternal age. This is best explained by which of the following facts about oogenesis?
options: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of meiosis I for years until ovulation
Oogonia continue mitotic division throughout adult life
Sperm mitochondria persist and increase nondisjunction risk with paternal age
Meiosis II is completed before puberty in all oocytes
explanations: Correct: primary oocytes form in utero and arrest in prophase of meiosis I, resuming only at ovulation, sometimes decades later; this prolonged arrest is thought to increase the risk of errors in chromosome segregation (nondisjunction) with advancing maternal age.
Incorrect: oogonia do not continue mitotic division throughout adult life; primary oocytes are formed prenatally and do not undergo further rounds of cell division until meiosis resumes at ovulation.
Incorrect: this question addresses maternal age-related risk from prolonged meiosis I arrest in oocytes, not paternal or sperm-related factors.
Incorrect: meiosis II is not completed until fertilization occurs; oocytes arrest in metaphase of meiosis II after ovulation, and completion happens only after fertilization.
questions.overview: Primary oocytes are formed prenatally and arrested in prophase of meiosis I until ovulation, which may occur decades later; this prolonged arrest is believed to underlie the increased risk of meiotic nondisjunction (and resulting trisomies such as Down syndrome) with advanced maternal age. Most trisomy 21 cases arise from maternal meiosis I nondisjunction.

questions.stem: A woman at 16 weeks' gestation undergoes a quad screen with results showing decreased AFP, decreased estriol, increased β-hCG, and increased inhibin A. Ultrasound at a subsequent visit shows a fetus with a flat facial profile, prominent epicanthal folds, and an atrioventricular septal defect. Which of the following mechanisms most likely accounts for this fetus's chromosomal abnormality?
options: Meiosis I nondisjunction in the mother
Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 15 inherited from the father
Balanced reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 21 and 22
Mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization leading to mosaicism
explanations: Correct: Down syndrome is caused by meiotic nondisjunction in ~95% of cases, 90% of these occurring in meiosis I, with the extra chromosome maternal in origin in 90% of cases; this quad screen pattern (↓AFP, ↓estriol, ↑β-hCG, ↑inhibin A) is classic for Down syndrome.

Incorrect: Robertsonian translocation causes only 2-3% of Down syndrome cases, is not associated with advanced maternal age, and has high familial recurrence risk; nothing in this vignette suggests translocation (no family history given).

Incorrect: deletion of 15q is the mechanism of Prader-Willi syndrome, not Down syndrome; the features described (flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, AV septal defect) are classic Down syndrome, not Prader-Willi.

Incorrect: balanced reciprocal translocations do not cause a trisomy 21 phenotype in the carrier; an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation (not reciprocal) is the translocation form implicated in Down syndrome.

Incorrect: mitotic error causing somatic mosaicism accounts for <2% of Down syndrome and typically produces milder features; the most common mechanism, especially without additional clues, is meiotic nondisjunction.
questions.overview: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is most commonly caused by meiotic nondisjunction (95%), usually in meiosis I, with the extra chromosome maternal in origin in 90% of cases; risk increases with advanced maternal age. Classic features include a flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease, hypotonia, and endocardial cushion defects. Second-trimester quad screen shows ↓AFP, ↓estriol, ↑β-hCG, and ↑inhibin A.

questions.stem: A child with intellectual disability has an elfin facial appearance, is unusually friendly and talkative with strangers, and is found to have supravalvular aortic stenosis. Deletion of a gene coding for which protein is most likely responsible?
explanations: Correct: Williams syndrome results from a partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7 that includes the elastin gene, causing elastin haploinsufficiency; this produces the elfin facial appearance, an unusually friendly ('cocktail party') personality, and vascular manifestations including supravalvular aortic stenosis.
Incorrect: dystrophin deficiency causes Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy, a muscle disorder unrelated to Williams syndrome's facial and cardiovascular features.
Incorrect: frataxin deficiency causes Friedreich's ataxia, a mitochondrial/neurologic disorder unrelated to Williams syndrome.
Incorrect: fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, which involves connective tissue and aortic root dilation, but is not the deletion syndrome described here.
questions.overview: Williams syndrome results from a microdeletion on chromosome 7q that includes the elastin gene, producing an 'elfin' facial appearance, intellectual disability with strong verbal skills, an unusually friendly personality toward strangers, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and mild hypercalcemia related to increased vitamin D sensitivity.

questions.stem: A newborn develops tetany and is found to have a serum calcium of 6.5 mg/dL. Echocardiogram reveals truncus arteriosus. Over the following months, the infant has recurrent viral and fungal infections. Which of the following is the most likely underlying genetic abnormality?
options: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
Microdeletion of chromosome 7 involving the elastin gene
Trinucleotide repeat expansion on the X chromosome
explanations: Incorrect: deletion of chromosome 5p causes cri-du-chat syndrome, characterized by a cat-like cry and intellectual disability, not immunodeficiency/hypocalcemia.
Incorrect: trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) does not classically cause thymic aplasia/hypocalcemia; heart defects are typically endocardial cushion defects, not conotruncal defects.
Incorrect: deletion involving the elastin gene on chromosome 7 causes Williams syndrome, with supravalvular aortic stenosis and hypercalcemia (not hypocalcemia).
Correct: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) causes thymic aplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency → viral/fungal infections), hypocalcemia (parathyroid aplasia), and conotruncal heart defects.
Incorrect: trinucleotide repeat disorders (e.g., Fragile X) are unrelated to this presentation of immunodeficiency, hypocalcemia, and heart defects.
questions.overview: DiGeorge (velocardiofacial) syndrome results from a 22q11 microdeletion causing thymic aplasia (T-cell deficiency with recurrent viral/fungal infections), parathyroid hypoplasia (hypocalcemia/tetany), and conotruncal cardiac anomalies. It is one of the classic microdeletion syndromes, along with cri-du-chat (5p) and Williams syndrome (7q, elastin gene).

questions.stem: Two genes on the same chromosome are found to recombine with a frequency (θ) of 0.5. This finding is most consistent with which of the following?
options: The genes are functionally unlinked, behaving as if on separate chromosomes
The genes are very close together and rarely recombine
The genes are in complete linkage disequilibrium
The genes have undergone a Robertsonian translocation
explanations: Correct: a recombination frequency of 0.5 indicates the genes assort as if unlinked (equivalent to being on separate chromosomes), the maximum possible value of θ.
Incorrect: genes located very close together have a low recombination frequency (θ close to 0), not 0.5.
Incorrect: linkage disequilibrium refers to non-random association of alleles in a population, a distinct concept from recombination frequency between two loci.
Incorrect: Robertsonian translocation is a structural chromosomal rearrangement unrelated to recombination frequency between two genes.
questions.overview: Recombination frequency (θ) reflects the physical distance between two loci: values near 0 indicate tight linkage (genes rarely separate during meiosis), while a value of 0.5 indicates the genes assort independently, as if on different chromosomes. Family-based recombination frequency data are used to construct linkage maps.

questions.stem: Retinitis pigmentosa can be caused by mutations at more than 40 different chromosomal loci, all producing a similar clinical phenotype of progressive visual impairment. This is best described as an example of:
explanations: Incorrect: codominance describes simultaneous phenotypic expression of two alleles at a single locus, unrelated to multiple disease-causing loci.

Incorrect: allelic heterogeneity refers to different mutations within the same gene/locus (as in beta-thalassemia or cystic fibrosis) producing a spectrum of disease, not mutations at entirely different loci.
Incorrect: incomplete penetrance describes gene carriers who fail to manifest disease at all, unrelated to the number of loci implicated in a phenotype.
Correct: locus heterogeneity refers to mutations at different genes (loci) producing the same phenotype, exactly as described for retinitis pigmentosa with mutations at over 40 different loci.
questions.overview: Locus heterogeneity means mutations at different genes can cause the same phenotype (e.g., retinitis pigmentosa, over 40 loci), while allelic heterogeneity means different mutations within the same gene cause a phenotype spectrum (e.g., beta-thalassemia, cystic fibrosis). Both explain why a single named 'disease' often has multiple distinct genetic causes.

questions.stem: Patients with Down syndrome are at high risk of developing Alzheimer's disease at an unusually early age (often in their 50s). This is best explained by which of the following?
options: Expansion of a CAG repeat in the HTT gene
Triplication of the DMD gene on the X chromosome
Triplication of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene located on chromosome 21
Deletion of the elastin gene on chromosome 7
explanations: Incorrect: CAG repeat expansion in HTT causes Huntington's disease, a distinct neurodegenerative condition not related to the chromosome 21 trisomy mechanism described in Down syndrome.
Incorrect: the DMD gene on the X chromosome encodes dystrophin and is implicated in muscular dystrophy, not Alzheimer's disease or Down syndrome pathology.

Correct: the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene is located on chromosome 21; trisomy 21 results in three copies of APP, increased amyloid precursor protein production, and accelerated amyloid plaque formation, explaining the early-onset Alzheimer's disease seen in Down syndrome.
Incorrect: deletion of the elastin gene on chromosome 7 causes Williams syndrome and is unrelated to Alzheimer's disease risk.
questions.overview: The amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene resides on chromosome 21; because Down syndrome involves trisomy of this chromosome, patients have an extra copy of APP, leading to increased amyloid-beta production, early amyloid plaque formation, and a markedly increased risk of Alzheimer's disease, typically presenting by the patient's 50s.

questions.stem: Genomic imprinting, in which only the maternally or paternally inherited copy of certain genes is expressed, is established during gametogenesis primarily through which epigenetic mechanism?
explanations: Incorrect: trinucleotide repeat expansion is the mechanism behind disorders like Huntington's disease and Fragile X syndrome, not genomic imprinting.
Correct: imprinting occurs via methylation of cytosine residues in DNA during gametogenesis, marking genes as maternal or paternal in origin and silencing one parental allele after fertilization.
Incorrect: nondisjunction is an error in chromosome segregation causing aneuploidy, unrelated to the epigenetic marking of imprinted genes.

Incorrect: X chromosome inactivation (lyonization) silences one X chromosome in females and is a distinct epigenetic process from autosomal genomic imprinting, though it also involves methylation/heterochromatin formation.
questions.overview: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic process, established during gametogenesis via DNA (cytosine) methylation, that marks genes as parent-of-origin specific so that only one parental allele is expressed after fertilization. Loss of the normally expressed allele in an imprinted region — as in Prader-Willi (paternal) or Angelman (maternal) syndrome — causes disease even though the other, silenced copy remains structurally intact.

questions.stem: A child has both copies of chromosome 7 inherited from the father, with no maternal contribution, but has a normal chromosome number (46) and no signs of aneuploidy. This scenario describes which of the following?
options: Meiosis II nondisjunction resulting in trisomy
explanations: Incorrect: Lyonization refers to X-chromosome inactivation in females, an unrelated epigenetic process from autosomal uniparental disomy.

Correct: uniparental disomy occurs when a child inherits two copies of a chromosome from one parent and none from the other, resulting in a normal (euploid) chromosome number but abnormal parental origin, which can unmask recessive disease alleles or disrupt imprinted genes.
Incorrect: meiosis II nondisjunction leading to trisomy would result in an abnormal (47) chromosome count, whereas this scenario specifically describes a normal chromosome number (46).

Incorrect: Robertsonian translocation is a structural fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes, a distinct mechanism from uniparental disomy, and typically results in either a balanced carrier state or aneuploidy, not a euploid two-copies-from-one-parent scenario.
questions.overview: Uniparental disomy occurs when both copies of a chromosome come from a single parent, leaving the child euploid (normal chromosome number) but with abnormal parental origin. This can be clinically silent, unmask recessive disease if the transmitting parent is a carrier, or disrupt imprinted gene expression (as in a subset of Prader-Willi syndrome cases from maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15).

questions.stem: In a family pedigree, hemophilia A affects only males across multiple generations, is transmitted through unaffected carrier daughters of affected men, and is never passed from an affected father to his son. This pattern is most consistent with which mode of inheritance?
explanations: Correct: X-linked recessive inheritance (as in hemophilia A and B) shows no male-to-male transmission (fathers always pass a Y chromosome to sons), affected males, and carrier (usually unaffected) daughters who can pass the disease to about half of their sons.
Incorrect: mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted exclusively through the mother to all offspring (both sexes), not this male-predominant sex-linked pattern with carrier daughters.
Incorrect: X-linked dominant inheritance would cause affected heterozygous females to also show disease, not just serve as unaffected carriers.
Incorrect: autosomal dominant inheritance would show affected individuals in both sexes across generations with male-to-male transmission possible, unlike this X-linked pattern.
questions.overview: X-linked recessive disorders (e.g., hemophilia A/B) affect males far more often than females, show no male-to-male transmission (since fathers give sons a Y chromosome), and are transmitted through typically unaffected carrier females, whose sons each have a 50% chance of being affected.

questions.stem: In a population, allele A has a frequency of 0.5 and allele B (at a separate but nearby locus) has a frequency of 0.9. The observed population frequency of the AB haplotype is 0.75, much higher than the 0.45 expected under random association. This finding best illustrates which of the following?
explanations: Incorrect: locus heterogeneity refers to mutations at different genes causing the same phenotype, not the statistical association between alleles at different loci.
Incorrect: genetic anticipation refers to worsening disease severity/earlier onset in successive generations, seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders, unrelated to haplotype frequency.

Correct: when a haplotype's observed population frequency differs from that predicted by multiplying individual allele frequencies, this is linkage disequilibrium, often reflecting recent mutation, close genetic distance, or population-specific history.

Incorrect: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes genotype frequencies at a single locus under set assumptions, not haplotype associations between two loci, and this scenario shows a deviation from expected independent association.
questions.overview: Linkage disequilibrium occurs when specific alleles at two nearby loci are inherited together more (or less) often than predicted by their individual population frequencies. It is greatest when a mutation is new to a population and fades over successive generations as recombination separates the loci, especially when the loci are farther apart.

questions.stem: A phenotypically normal woman with 45 chromosomes on karyotype, including a fused chromosome 14;21, has a child with Down syndrome. Compared to Down syndrome caused by simple meiotic nondisjunction, this translocation-associated form is characterized by which of the following?
options: No association with advanced maternal age and high familial recurrence risk
Strong association with advanced maternal age and low recurrence risk
Occurrence exclusively in sporadic, non-familial cases
explanations: Incorrect: mosaic distribution of trisomic cells describes the rare mitotic-error form of Down syndrome (<2% of cases), not the translocation mechanism.

Correct: Robertsonian translocation-associated Down syndrome accounts for only 2-3% of cases, is not associated with advanced maternal age, and carries a high recurrence risk within families because a balanced carrier parent can repeatedly transmit an unbalanced translocation.
Incorrect: this describes typical meiotic nondisjunction Down syndrome (95% of cases), which is associated with maternal age, not the translocation form.
Incorrect: translocation-associated Down syndrome is notable specifically for its familial (heritable) recurrence pattern, the opposite of 'exclusively sporadic.'
questions.overview: Robertsonian translocation causes only 2-3% of Down syndrome cases (most commonly fusion with chromosome 14), is not linked to advanced maternal age, and carries a high recurrence risk in families because a phenotypically normal balanced carrier parent (45 chromosomes) can pass an unbalanced translocation to multiple offspring.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with vaginal bleeding. Examination shows large, irregularly bordered ('coast of Maine') hyperpigmented skin macules and a leg deformity from fibrous bone lesions. Genetic testing reveals a mutation of the GNAS gene present in only some tissues, not all cells of the body. Which of the following best explains this pattern of genetic involvement?
options: A germline mutation transmitted from an affected parent
Meiotic nondisjunction producing trisomy of the affected chromosome
A postzygotic somatic mutation occurring after fertilization, producing tissue mosaicism
X-linked dominant inheritance with skewed lyonization
explanations: Incorrect: McCune-Albright syndrome is not inherited from a parent; it arises sporadically from a new somatic mutation after fertilization, and a germline mutation affecting the whole body is not compatible with survival.
Incorrect: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by a point mutation in GNAS with mosaic distribution, not aneuploidy from meiotic nondisjunction.

Correct: McCune-Albright syndrome results from a sporadic, postzygotic (occurring after fertilization) somatic mutation in the GNAS gene, leading to mosaicism where only some tissues carry the mutation; a germline (whole-body) mutation is lethal, so surviving patients always show a mosaic pattern.
Incorrect: McCune-Albright syndrome is due to a somatic (postzygotic) mutation, not X-linked inheritance with lyonization, which applies to X-linked disorders in females.
Incorrect: maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 is a mechanism of Prader-Willi syndrome, unrelated to McCune-Albright syndrome's GNAS mutation.
questions.overview: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by a sporadic, postzygotic somatic mutation in the GNAS gene (constitutively activating the Gs-alpha subunit and increasing cAMP signaling), producing tissue mosaicism. It classically presents with precocious puberty, café-au-lait skin macules with irregular ('coast of Maine') borders, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia; a germline form of the mutation would be lethal.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has severe intellectual disability, an ataxic gait, and frequent unprovoked laughter and smiling. She has a history of seizures. Genetic testing reveals a deletion of the maternal copy of chromosome 15q11-q13. Which gene's loss of expression is most directly responsible for this phenotype?
explanations: Incorrect: ELN encodes elastin and is deleted in Williams syndrome, not Angelman syndrome.
Incorrect: DMD encodes dystrophin and is implicated in Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy, unrelated to this presentation.
Incorrect: FMR1 is the gene implicated in Fragile X syndrome, not Angelman syndrome.

Correct: UBE3A is normally expressed only from the maternal chromosome 15; its loss (via maternal deletion, the majority mechanism) causes Angelman syndrome, with severe intellectual disability, ataxia, seizures, and a 'happy puppet' demeanor.
Incorrect: HTT is the huntingtin gene implicated in Huntington's disease, a distinct adult-onset movement disorder.
questions.overview: Angelman syndrome results from loss of expression of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene on chromosome 15q11-q13, most often due to a maternal deletion. Clinical features include severe intellectual disability, ataxia, frequent seizures, and a characteristic happy demeanor with inappropriate laughter ('happy puppet' syndrome).

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man develops chorea and progressive dementia. His father had similar symptoms beginning at age 55. Genetic testing shows an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene, with a greater number of repeats in the son than was present in the father. This phenomenon of worsening severity and earlier onset in successive generations is known as:
explanations: Incorrect: linkage disequilibrium refers to the non-random association of alleles at different loci in a population, unrelated to changes in repeat length across generations within a family.

Correct: anticipation refers to the phenomenon, seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington's disease, in which disease severity worsens and age of onset decreases in successive generations due to further expansion of an unstable repeat.
Incorrect: incomplete penetrance refers to some gene carriers failing to manifest disease entirely, a distinct concept from progressively earlier onset across generations.
Incorrect: genetic heterogeneity refers to the same phenotype being caused by different genes or mutations, not to changing repeat length and severity across generations of the same family.
questions.overview: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by CAG (polyglutamine) repeat expansion in the HTT gene, leading to basal ganglia (striatal) degeneration with chorea and dementia, typically presenting in the 30s-40s. Trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington's disease exhibit anticipation, where repeat number tends to increase across generations, causing earlier onset and greater severity in offspring.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has moderate intellectual disability, a long narrow face with large protruding ears, and macroorchidism. His maternal uncle has similar features. Genetic testing shows an expansion of a trinucleotide repeat beyond 200 copies in a gene on the X chromosome, resulting in gene silencing by DNA methylation. Which of the following best describes the mode of inheritance and repeat sequence involved?
options: X-linked dominant inheritance with CGG repeat expansion in FMR1
Autosomal recessive inheritance with GAA repeat expansion
Autosomal dominant inheritance with CAG repeat expansion in HTT
X-linked recessive inheritance with CTG repeat expansion
Mitochondrial inheritance with CCTG repeat expansion
explanations: Correct: Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion (>200 repeats = full mutation) in the FMR1 gene, leading to methylation and gene silencing; features include intellectual disability, a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism, more severe in males.
Incorrect: GAA repeat expansion with autosomal recessive inheritance describes Friedreich's ataxia (frataxin gene), a distinct disorder causing ataxia and cardiomyopathy, not this phenotype.

Incorrect: CAG repeat expansion with autosomal dominant inheritance describes Huntington's disease (HTT gene), which causes an adult-onset movement disorder, not this childhood intellectual disability syndrome.
Incorrect: CTG repeat expansion describes myotonic dystrophy type I (DMPK gene), an autosomal dominant muscle disorder, not this X-linked condition.
Incorrect: CCTG (tetranucleotide) repeat expansion describes myotonic dystrophy type 2 (CNBP gene), which is autosomal dominant, not mitochondrial, and is unrelated to this presentation.
questions.overview: Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder caused by CGG repeat expansion (>200 repeats) in FMR1, leading to methylation-induced gene silencing. It is the second most common genetic cause of intellectual disability (after Down syndrome) and classically presents with a long face, large ears/jaw, macroorchidism, and autism spectrum features, more severe in males.

questions.stem: An autosomal recessive disease occurs in 1 in 4,900 newborns in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the approximate frequency of carriers (heterozygotes) in this population?
explanations: Incorrect: 14% is off by a factor of 10 from the correct carrier frequency calculation.
Incorrect: 1.4% corresponds to q itself (the disease allele frequency), not the carrier (heterozygote) frequency, which is approximately 2q.
Incorrect: 50% would be far too high for a rare autosomal recessive disease and does not follow from the Hardy-Weinberg calculation.
Correct: q² = 1/4900, so q = 1/70 ≈ 0.0143; p ≈ 1 − 0.0143 ≈ 0.986; carrier frequency = 2pq ≈ 2(0.986)(0.0143) ≈ 0.028, or about 2.7-2.8%, consistent with the approximation 2q for rare diseases.
questions.overview: For autosomal recessive diseases in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, disease frequency = q², so q = √(disease frequency). Carrier frequency = 2pq, which for rare diseases (p close to 1) approximates 2q. This calculation is high-yield for estimating carrier rates from known disease prevalence.

questions.stem: A single gene mutation in a patient with Marfan syndrome leads to lens dislocation, aortic root dilation, and long limbs with joint laxity. This phenomenon, in which one gene mutation produces multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects, is termed:
explanations: Incorrect: locus heterogeneity refers to mutations at different genetic loci causing the same disease phenotype, the opposite relationship from one gene causing many effects.

Correct: pleiotropy is defined as a single gene mutation producing effects on multiple organ systems/traits, exactly as seen in Marfan syndrome (eyes, aorta, skeleton) from a single fibrillin-1 mutation.
Incorrect: incomplete penetrance refers to some gene carriers not manifesting disease at all, not a single gene affecting multiple organ systems.
Incorrect: codominance refers to simultaneous expression of two different alleles at one locus, unrelated to multi-system effects of a single mutation.
questions.overview: Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene mutation produces effects across multiple, seemingly unrelated organ systems or traits. Classic examples include Marfan syndrome (eyes, aorta, skeleton), phenylketonuria (skin, body odor, cognition), and cystic fibrosis (lungs, pancreas).

questions.stem: The dystrophin protein, which is deficient in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, normally functions to:
options: Transport neurotransmitters across the neuromuscular junction
Regulate calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Catalyze ATP hydrolysis during muscle contraction
Anchor intracellular actin to the extracellular matrix via a transmembrane dystroglycan complex
explanations: Dystrophin is a structural protein maintaining muscle membrane integrity, not a neurotransmitter transporter at the neuromuscular junction.
Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is regulated by the ryanodine receptor and related channels, not dystrophin.
ATP hydrolysis during contraction is performed by myosin ATPase, not dystrophin.

Correct — dystrophin connects intracellular actin filaments to alpha- and beta-dystroglycan in the muscle cell membrane, which in turn connects to the extracellular matrix (laminin), maintaining sarcolemmal integrity during contraction.
questions.overview: Dystrophin is a large cytoskeletal protein that maintains muscle membrane stability by linking intracellular actin to the transmembrane dystroglycan complex, which connects to the extracellular matrix (laminin). Loss of dystrophin (Duchenne) or production of a partially functional truncated form (Becker) leads to progressive myonecrosis, muscle weakness, and elevated muscle enzymes such as creatine kinase.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man reports difficulty releasing his grip after shaking hands and progressive weakness in his hands and face. On exam, he has a long, narrow face with temporal wasting, frontal balding, and bilateral cataracts. ECG shows first-degree AV block. He also reports decreased libido, and exam reveals testicular atrophy. Which of the following best describes the genetic mechanism underlying this disorder?
options: CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene, autosomal dominant
CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene, autosomal dominant
GAA repeat expansion in the frataxin gene, autosomal recessive
Deletion in the DMD gene, X-linked recessive
CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, X-linked dominant
explanations: CAG repeat expansion in HTT causes Huntington's disease, which presents with chorea and dementia, not myotonia and cataracts.

Correct — Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is caused by a CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the DMPK gene on chromosome 19, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, producing myotonia, cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac conduction disease, and hypogonadism.
GAA repeat expansion in frataxin causes Friedreich's ataxia, an autosomal recessive ataxic disorder, not myotonic dystrophy.
DMD gene deletions cause Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy, X-linked recessive disorders without myotonia or cataracts.
CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 causes Fragile X syndrome, an X-linked disorder with intellectual disability, not this adult myopathy/cataract syndrome.
questions.overview: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide (CTG) repeat expansion disorder in the DMPK gene on chromosome 19. It is the most common adult-onset muscular dystrophy, presenting with myotonia (inability to relax muscles after contraction), a characteristic long face with frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and primary hypogonadism with testicular atrophy.

questions.stem: A female infant is born small for gestational age with a birth weight well below the 10th percentile. Exam reveals a prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched fists with the index finger overlapping the third digit, and rocker-bottom feet. Echocardiogram reveals a ventricular septal defect. Which of the following is the most likely underlying chromosomal abnormality?
explanations: Correct — Trisomy 18 (Edward syndrome) presents with intrauterine growth restriction, a prominent occiput, micrognathia, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart disease; most affected infants die within the first year.
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) presents with flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, and endocardial cushion defects, not clenched fists with overlapping fingers or rocker-bottom feet.
Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) presents with microphthalmia, cleft lip/palate, and postaxial polydactyly rather than the overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet described here.
47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) presents in males later in life with hypogonadism, not with these neonatal dysmorphic features.
45,X (Turner syndrome) occurs in phenotypic females with webbed neck and lymphedema, not the growth restriction and limb findings described.
questions.overview: Edward syndrome (trisomy 18) is the second most common autosomal trisomy in live births, most often due to meiotic nondisjunction and associated with advanced maternal age. Classic features include severe intrauterine growth restriction, a small head with a prominent occiput, micrognathia, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet, along with a high rate of congenital heart and GI defects. Prognosis is poor, with most infants dying in the first weeks to year of life.

questions.stem: A child is found to have two structurally different homologous copies of chromosome 15 inherited from the same parent (uniparental heterodisomy), with no contribution from the other parent. This finding is most consistent with a nondisjunction error occurring during which stage of gametogenesis?
explanations: A mitotic error after fertilization would typically produce mosaicism (a mixture of normal and abnormal cell lines) rather than uniform heterodisomy in all cells.
Meiosis II nondisjunction involves failure of sister chromatids (which are genetically identical, aside from crossover) to separate, producing isodisomy (two identical copies), not heterodisomy.
Fertilization itself is the union of two normal or abnormal gametes; it is not the point at which nondisjunction of homologous chromosomes occurs.

Correct — heterodisomy (inheritance of both different homologous chromosomes from one parent) results from failure of homologous chromosomes to separate during meiosis I, before sister chromatids have differentiated genetically.
questions.overview: Uniparental disomy occurs when both copies of a chromosome pair come from one parent, with no contribution from the other. Heterodisomy (two different homologous chromosomes from one parent) implicates a meiosis I error, since homologous chromosomes have not yet been separated; isodisomy (two identical copies) implicates a meiosis II error, since it involves duplicated sister chromatids. This distinction helps localize the stage of nondisjunction in cases like Prader-Willi syndrome from maternal uniparental disomy.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with a several-day history of oral thrush and a prior episode of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Echocardiogram performed in the newborn period showed tetralogy of Fallot. Laboratory studies reveal markedly reduced CD3+ T lymphocytes with normal B lymphocyte counts. Genetic testing reveals a microdeletion. Which of the following is the most likely underlying chromosomal abnormality?
options: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7
Microdeletion of the paternal copy of chromosome 15q11-13
Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 22
explanations: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) causes holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, and cleft lip/palate, not isolated T-cell deficiency.
Cri-du-chat (5p deletion) causes cat-like cry, microcephaly, and intellectual disability, not thymic/cardiac/T-cell defects.
Williams syndrome (7q deletion, elastin gene) causes supravalvular aortic stenosis and elfin facies, not immunodeficiency.
Paternal 15q11-13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome (hypotonia, hyperphagia), unrelated to immune/cardiac defects.
Correct — 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge/thymic aplasia) causes T-cell deficiency from thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcemia, and conotruncal cardiac defects like tetralogy of Fallot.
questions.overview: DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia) results from a 22q11.2 microdeletion causing failure of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches to develop, producing the triad of T-cell immunodeficiency (thymic hypoplasia), hypocalcemia (parathyroid hypoplasia), and conotruncal cardiac defects (tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus). It is also known as velocardiofacial or Shprintzen syndrome. Recurrent viral/fungal infections reflect the T-cell deficit.

questions.stem: A population geneticist is evaluating whether a population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Which of the following observations would suggest that the population violates the assumptions required for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
options: Individuals mate randomly with respect to the genotype in question
Individuals with a certain genotype preferentially choose mates with the same genotype (assortative mating)
There is no migration into or out of the population
explanations: Random mating is one of the required assumptions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, so this observation would support, not violate, equilibrium.
Correct — nonrandom (assortative) mating violates the random mating assumption required for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, causing allele and genotype frequencies to deviate from predicted values.
Absence of migration is a required assumption for equilibrium, so this observation supports rather than violates it.
A large population size is a required assumption (to minimize genetic drift), so this supports equilibrium rather than violating it.
questions.overview: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium requires a large population, completely random mating, no new mutations, no migration in or out of the population, and no natural selection. When these assumptions hold, allele frequencies (p, q) and genotype frequencies (p2, 2pq, q2) remain stable across generations; violation of any assumption (e.g., nonrandom mating, small population size, selection) can shift allele and genotype frequencies over time.

questions.stem: On eye examination of a newborn with suspected Down syndrome, small white or grayish spots are noted arranged around the periphery of the iris. These findings are known as:
explanations: Lisch nodules are pigmented iris hamartomas seen in neurofibromatosis type 1, not Down syndrome.
Correct — Brushfield spots are white or light-colored spots on the periphery of the iris, a classic ocular finding associated with Down syndrome.
Roth spots are retinal hemorrhages with pale centers seen in infective endocarditis, not an iris finding in Down syndrome.
Koplik spots are small white lesions on the buccal mucosa seen in measles, unrelated to the iris or Down syndrome.
questions.overview: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is associated with characteristic dysmorphic features including a flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, upslanting palpebral fissures, Brushfield spots (white iris spots), a single transverse palmar crease, and a 'sandal gap' between the first and second toes, in addition to hypotonia, short stature, and an increased risk of congenital heart and GI anomalies.

questions.stem: A young child develops osteosarcoma, and genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene. Family history reveals early-onset sarcomas, breast cancer, leukemia, and adrenal tumors across multiple generations. This pattern of cancer predisposition is best explained by which of the following?
options: X-linked recessive inheritance of a DNA repair gene defect
Li-Fraumeni syndrome, following a two-hit mechanism of tumor suppressor gene inactivation
Mitochondrial inheritance of a nuclear-encoded tumor suppressor gene
Genomic imprinting of the TP53 gene
explanations: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is autosomal dominant, not X-linked recessive, and TP53 is a cell-cycle regulator, not primarily a DNA mismatch repair gene (that would describe Lynch syndrome).

Correct — Li-Fraumeni syndrome results from a germline TP53 mutation and follows the two-hit hypothesis, in which a somatic mutation inactivating the remaining allele leads to malignancy; it causes sarcomas, breast cancer, leukemia, and adrenal tumors (the 'SBLA' cancer syndrome) at an early age.
TP53 mutations follow classic autosomal dominant Mendelian inheritance via nuclear chromosomes, not maternal mitochondrial inheritance.
TP53 is not known to be an imprinted gene; both alleles are normally expressed, and disease follows a two-hit tumor suppressor mechanism, not parent-of-origin-specific expression.
questions.overview: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by a germline mutation in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene, which normally delays cell cycle progression to allow DNA repair. As with other tumor suppressor gene disorders, it follows the two-hit hypothesis: carriers are born with one mutant allele in every cell, and a single additional somatic mutation in the remaining allele is sufficient to trigger malignancy, producing early-onset sarcomas, breast cancer, leukemia, and adrenal cortical tumors.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for a heart murmur. Echocardiography reveals narrowing of the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve. Laboratory testing shows an elevated serum calcium level. She has well-developed verbal skills for her age but delayed motor milestones, and is noted by her parents to be unusually sociable with strangers. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely responsible for this presentation?
options: Deletion of the elastin gene on chromosome 7
Trinucleotide CGG repeat expansion on the X chromosome
explanations: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) causes different dysmorphic features and endocardial cushion defects, not supravalvular aortic stenosis or hypercalcemia.
Paternal 15q11-13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome, characterized by hypotonia and hyperphagia, not this cardiac/personality phenotype.

Correct — Williams syndrome results from a microdeletion on chromosome 7q that includes the elastin gene, producing supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia, and a friendly, verbally skilled personality with elfin facies.
CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 causes Fragile X syndrome, associated with macroorchidism and autistic features, not supravalvular aortic stenosis or hypercalcemia.
22q11.2 deletion causes DiGeorge syndrome with immunodeficiency and hypocalcemia (not hypercalcemia).
questions.overview: Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 7q that includes the elastin gene, leading to connective tissue elastin haploinsufficiency. Classic features include an 'elfin' facial appearance, supravalvular aortic stenosis (and other arteriopathies), mild-moderate intellectual disability with strong verbal skills, an extremely friendly/sociable personality, and mild hypercalcemia related to increased vitamin D sensitivity.

questions.stem: Two gene loci on the same chromosome are found to have a recombination frequency (θ) close to zero in family linkage studies. This finding indicates that the two loci are:
options: Located very close together on the chromosome
Located far apart on the chromosome
explanations: Correct — recombination frequency is proportional to distance; a θ near zero indicates the loci are very close together and rarely separated by crossover (tight linkage).
Frequent independent assortment produces a recombination frequency near 0.5, the opposite of what is described.
Loci located far apart would have a higher recombination frequency, approaching 0.5, not close to zero.
Loci on different chromosomes assort independently and would show a recombination frequency of 0.5, not near zero.
questions.overview: Recombination frequency (θ) reflects the physical distance between two loci on a chromosome, ranging from 0 (perfectly linked, no recombination) to 0.5 (unlinked, behaving as if on separate chromosomes due to independent assortment). Family linkage studies use recombination frequency to construct genetic maps, since closely spaced genes are rarely separated by crossover events during meiosis.

questions.stem: Angelman syndrome results from loss of expression of the UBE3A gene. Under normal conditions, which parental copy of UBE3A is expressed in the brain?
options: Both maternal and paternal copies equally
explanations: UBE3A is an imprinted gene, so it does not show biallelic expression; only the maternal copy is normally active in the brain.
The paternal copy of UBE3A is normally silenced (not expressed) in the brain; deletion of the paternal chromosome 15 region instead causes Prader-Willi syndrome.
UBE3A is normally actively expressed from the maternal allele; it is not silenced on both chromosomes under normal circumstances.

Correct — UBE3A is normally expressed only from the maternally inherited chromosome 15 in the brain, so deletion or dysfunction of the maternal copy (as in Angelman syndrome) results in a complete lack of UBE3A expression.
questions.overview: Angelman syndrome results from loss of function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene within the 15q11-13 imprinted region, most commonly due to deletion of the maternal chromosome 15 segment (with maternal uniparental disomy accounting for only a small minority of cases). Because the paternal copy of UBE3A is normally silenced in the brain, loss of the maternal copy leaves no functional UBE3A, producing severe intellectual disability, ataxia, seizures, and a characteristic happy demeanor with frequent laughter.

questions.stem: A secondary oocyte released at ovulation remains arrested at which stage of meiosis until fertilization occurs?
explanations: Secondary oocytes have already completed meiosis I by the time of ovulation, so they are not arrested in metaphase of meiosis I.
Correct — after completing meiosis I at ovulation, the secondary oocyte begins meiosis II but arrests in metaphase II until fertilization triggers completion of meiosis.
The oocyte does not reach anaphase of meiosis II until after fertilization occurs; it is arrested earlier, at metaphase II.
Primary oocytes, not secondary oocytes, are arrested in prophase of meiosis I, from fetal life until puberty.
questions.overview: Oogenesis begins in utero, with primary oocytes arrested in prophase of meiosis I until puberty. Each cycle, a primary oocyte completes meiosis I, forming a secondary oocyte and a polar body; the secondary oocyte then begins meiosis II but arrests again in metaphase II. Fertilization is required to trigger completion of meiosis II, underscoring why meiosis I errors are especially common with advancing maternal age given the decades-long arrest.

questions.stem: Beta-thalassemia can result from a wide range of different mutations within the beta-globin gene, with mutations that abolish all protein function (β0) causing more severe disease than mutations that only partially reduce function (β+). This phenomenon, in which different mutations at the same locus produce a spectrum of disease severity, is termed:
explanations: Locus heterogeneity refers to mutations at different genes/loci causing the same disease (e.g., retinitis pigmentosa), not multiple mutations within a single gene.
Correct — allelic heterogeneity describes multiple different mutations within the same gene (locus) producing a spectrum of disease severity, as seen with beta-thalassemia and cystic fibrosis.
Codominance describes simultaneous expression of two different alleles in a heterozygote (e.g., ABO blood groups), not a spectrum of severity from different mutations at one locus.
Genetic imprinting refers to parent-of-origin-specific gene expression, unrelated to the number of mutation types within a gene.
questions.overview: Allelic heterogeneity occurs when multiple different mutations at the same gene locus can cause the same general disease, often producing variable severity depending on the specific mutation's effect on protein function. Classic examples include beta-thalassemia (βo = no function vs β+ = partial function) and cystic fibrosis (CFTR gene, over 1400 described mutations).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common genetic mechanism underlying Prader-Willi syndrome?
options: Deletion of the maternally inherited copy of the 15q11-13 region
A CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion on the X chromosome
Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 in all cases
Deletion of the paternally inherited copy of the 15q11-13 region
explanations: Deletion of the maternal 15q11-13 region causes Angelman syndrome (loss of maternally-expressed UBE3A), not Prader-Willi.
Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by an imprinting/deletion defect on chromosome 15, not a trinucleotide repeat expansion (that mechanism underlies Fragile X syndrome).
Maternal uniparental disomy accounts for only about 25% of Prader-Willi cases, making it a minority rather than the most common mechanism.
Correct — approximately 75% of Prader-Willi syndrome cases result from a sporadic deletion of the paternal copy of the 15q11-13 region, silencing paternally-expressed genes.
questions.overview: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of function of paternally-expressed genes in the 15q11-13 region, most commonly (~75%) due to a sporadic deletion of the paternal chromosome 15 segment, with the remainder due to maternal uniparental disomy (two maternal copies, no paternal copy). Clinical features include neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, followed by hyperphagia and obesity, mild intellectual disability, and hypogonadism.

questions.stem: Genomic imprinting, in which certain genes are expressed only from the maternally or paternally inherited chromosome, is established during gametogenesis primarily through which molecular mechanism?
options: Methylation of cytosine residues in DNA
explanations: Correct — imprinting occurs during gametogenesis when genes are 'marked' as maternal or paternal in origin through methylation of cytosine in DNA, which then silences one parental allele after fertilization.
X chromosome inactivation (lyonization) silences one X chromosome in females for dosage compensation, which is a related but distinct epigenetic phenomenon from autosomal genomic imprinting.
Trinucleotide repeat expansion underlies disorders like Fragile X and Huntington's disease, not the establishment of genomic imprinting.
Nondisjunction is a meiotic error causing aneuploidy, unrelated to the epigenetic marking process of imprinting.
questions.overview: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon in which a gene's expression depends on its parent of origin. During gametogenesis, genes are marked as paternal or maternal, typically via cytosine methylation, which silences one parental copy after fertilization. Only imprinted genes show this monoallelic expression; most genes are non-imprinted and express both alleles. Disruption of imprinted regions on chromosome 15q11-13 underlies Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presents for evaluation of infertility after 2 years of unprotected intercourse with his partner. Physical exam reveals small, firm testes, sparse facial hair, and gynecomastia. He has long arms and legs. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Laboratory studies show low serum testosterone with elevated FSH and LH. Which of the following karyotypes is most consistent with this presentation?
explanations: 45,X (Turner syndrome) occurs in phenotypic females, not males with a male reproductive presentation.
FMR1 CGG expansion causes Fragile X syndrome, associated with macroorchidism, not small testes and gynecomastia.
45,X/46,XX mosaicism describes mosaic Turner syndrome in phenotypic females.
47,XXX (triple X) occurs in females and is often clinically silent, not associated with a male infertility presentation.

Correct — Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary hypogonadism with small firm testes, elevated gonadotropins from loss of testosterone/inhibin B feedback, gynecomastia, and long limbs from the extra SHOX gene copy.
questions.overview: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common sex chromosome aneuploidy in males, usually from meiotic nondisjunction. It causes primary hypogonadism with small firm testes and seminiferous tubule atrophy, leading to low testosterone, infertility, and compensatory elevation of LH and FSH (loss of inhibin B feedback). Extra copies of the SHOX gene produce a tall, eunuchoid body habitus with long limbs; gynecomastia and learning disabilities are also common.

questions.stem: A female carrier of an X-linked recessive disease allele unexpectedly develops clinical manifestations of the disease, despite having one normal allele on her other X chromosome. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
options: Uniparental disomy of the X chromosome
Complete deletion of the Y chromosome
Random but skewed X-inactivation resulting in preferential inactivation of the X chromosome carrying the normal allele
A new spontaneous autosomal dominant mutation
explanations: Uniparental disomy involves inheriting both copies of a chromosome from one parent; it is not the mechanism underlying variable X-linked recessive expression in carrier females due to X-inactivation.
Females do not have a Y chromosome under normal circumstances, so its deletion is not relevant to this scenario.

Correct — Lyonization (X-inactivation) is normally random, but skewed lyonization can result in a majority of cells inactivating the X chromosome bearing the normal allele, unmasking the disease phenotype in a heterozygous female carrier.
The scenario describes an X-linked recessive condition already known to be present as a carrier state, not a new autosomal dominant mutation.
questions.overview: Lyonization is the random inactivation of one X chromosome in each cell of a female embryo early in development, creating a mosaic of cells expressing either the maternal or paternal X. While usually balanced, skewed lyonization (where a majority of cells inactivate the X carrying the normal allele) can cause female carriers of X-linked recessive diseases to manifest disease symptoms, unlike the typical unaffected carrier state.

questions.stem: Unlike Duchenne muscular dystrophy, in which about two-thirds of cases are inherited from a carrier mother, Becker muscular dystrophy cases are inherited from a carrier mother in approximately what proportion of cases?
explanations: 100% is not accurate, as a small proportion of Becker cases still arise from new mutations rather than maternal inheritance.
50% underestimates the proportion; Becker muscular dystrophy is inherited from a carrier mother in about 90% of cases.

Correct — approximately 90% of Becker muscular dystrophy cases are inherited from a carrier mother, a higher proportion than in Duchenne (two-thirds), reflecting differences in new mutation rates and reproductive fitness.
10% is far too low; the vast majority of Becker cases are inherited rather than arising from new mutations.
questions.overview: Both Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy are X-linked recessive disorders caused by mutations in the DMD gene, with Duchenne caused by frameshift mutations (absent or truncated dystrophin) and Becker caused by non-frameshift mutations (partially functional dystrophin, milder disease). Becker muscular dystrophy is inherited from a carrier mother in about 90% of cases, more often than Duchenne, and has a later onset with slower progression, often allowing survival into the 30s.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressive difficulty walking and frequent falls over the past year. Exam shows a wide-based, ataxic gait, dysarthria, loss of vibration and proprioception, and absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities. Echocardiogram reveals concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. He also has pes cavus and kyphoscoliosis. Genetic testing reveals an expanded trinucleotide repeat in a gene on chromosome 9. This condition is inherited in which of the following patterns, and involves a protein important for which cellular process?
explanations: The disorder is not autosomal dominant, and frataxin is not involved in microtubule transport.
Dystrophin-glycoprotein complex defects cause Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy, which are X-linked, not this disease.
Mitochondrial DNA mutations follow maternal inheritance, but Friedreich's ataxia is a nuclear (chromosome 9) gene defect with autosomal recessive inheritance.

Correct — Friedreich's ataxia is autosomal recessive, caused by GAA repeat expansion in the frataxin gene on chromosome 9; frataxin is a mitochondrial protein, and its deficiency causes mitochondrial dysfunction affecting the brain, heart, and pancreas.
DNA mismatch repair gene mutations cause Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), unrelated to Friedreich's ataxia.
questions.overview: Friedreich's ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide (GAA) repeat expansion disorder affecting the frataxin gene on chromosome 9. Frataxin is needed for normal mitochondrial function, and its deficiency causes progressive spinocerebellar and dorsal column degeneration (ataxia, loss of proprioception/vibration, areflexia), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and skeletal deformities like kyphoscoliosis and pes cavus, with onset in adolescence.

questions.stem: A disease-causing mutation arises near a specific allele of a nearby polymorphic marker. Over many subsequent generations, the degree of linkage disequilibrium between the mutation and the marker allele is expected to:
options: Decrease over time as recombination separates the loci
Increase steadily due to natural selection
Increase only if the population size decreases
Remain constant regardless of generations passed
explanations: Correct — linkage disequilibrium is greatest when a mutation first arises near a marker allele and fades over successive generations as recombination gradually separates the two loci.
Natural selection is not required for linkage disequilibrium to change; recombination alone erodes it over time.

A decrease in population size would tend to slow, not accelerate, decay by increasing genetic drift, but the fundamental cause of decay is recombination over time and distance, not a requirement for the population to shrink.
Linkage disequilibrium is not static — it decays as recombination events accumulate across generations.
questions.overview: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) refers to non-random association between alleles at nearby loci in a population, distinct from family-based linkage studies used for loci with larger recombination frequencies. LD is greatest immediately after a new mutation arises and fades over successive generations as recombination breaks up the ancestral haplotype; the rate of decay depends on the physical distance between loci and the number of generations elapsed.

questions.stem: Two unaffected parents have two children with the same rare autosomal dominant disorder. Genetic testing of the parents' blood and skin samples shows no evidence of the disease-causing mutation. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Somatic mosaicism in one of the affected children
Germline mosaicism in one of the parents
A new independent spontaneous mutation occurred in each child
explanations: Somatic mosaicism in the children would not explain why two separate children share the same specific mutation inherited from a parent.

Incomplete penetrance would apply if a parent carried the mutation but did not express the phenotype; the parents test negative on standard tissue sampling, favoring germline mosaicism over penetrance issues in the children (who are affected).

Correct — germline mosaicism occurs when a parent has the mutation only in a subset of germ cells (not in blood/skin), making it undetectable on standard testing while still being transmissible, and can present as recurrent 'sporadic' disease in multiple offspring.

While possible statistically, two independent identical spontaneous mutations in two separate children is far less likely than a single germline mosaic mutation transmitted from one parent's germ cell population.
